sections.section_title: Foundations: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, Drug-Associated Myopathy, and Immune-Mediated Necrotising Myopathy
sections.description: This section provides the core background needed to understand the case. It introduces semaglutide and related GLP-1 receptor agonists, reviews the spectrum of medication-related muscle injury, and explains the defining clinical, serologic, and histopathologic features of immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM), including seronegative disease.
subtopics: Clinical uses of GLP-1 receptor agonists in obesity, fatty liver disease, and type 2 diabetes
Common adverse effects of semaglutide and why severe systemic intolerance matters clinically
Muscle-related adverse events associated with GLP-1-based therapies: loss of lean mass, rhabdomyolysis, and the possibility of immune-triggered injury
Definition of IMNM and how it differs from polymyositis, dermatomyositis, and toxic myopathy
Typical presentation of IMNM: proximal weakness, dysphagia, dysphonia, and marked CK elevation
Autoantibody-associated IMNM subtypes: anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, and seronegative IMNM
Pathophysiology of necrotising myopathy: myofibre necrosis, regeneration, macrophage-predominant inflammation, and membrane attack complex deposition
Concept of drug-triggered autoimmunity and the precedent of statin-associated necrotising myopathy
Why seronegative IMNM is diagnostically challenging and clinically important

sections.section_title: From First Dose to Progressive Neuromuscular Syndrome: Reconstructing the Clinical Course
sections.description: This section walks through the patient’s presentation in chronological order and teaches learners how to recognize the evolving syndrome. It emphasizes the transition from an acute adverse reaction after semaglutide exposure to a delayed, progressive autoimmune-pattern myopathy with bulbar and proximal limb involvement.
subtopics: Baseline patient context: age, comorbid obesity, hepatosteatosis, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and prior venous thromboembolism
Pre-existing transaminase elevation and biopsy-proven NAFLD as an important source of diagnostic noise
Initiation of semaglutide for obesity and fatty liver disease
Immediate post-dose reaction: nausea, vomiting, poor intake, dyspnoea, acute kidney injury, and severe metabolic acidosis
Interpretation of the modest early CK elevation during the initial hospitalization
Progressive decline over 4 months despite discontinuation after a single dose
Red-flag symptoms suggesting inflammatory myopathy: inability to sit or stand independently, proximal weakness, dysphagia, and dysphonia
Physical examination pattern localizing disease to muscle rather than neuropathic or central causes
Recognition of severe disease features that heighten urgency: bulbar symptoms, major functional loss, and possible cardiac involvement

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Evaluation: Laboratory, Imaging, and Histopathologic Confirmation
sections.description: This section explains the workup step by step, showing how clinicians used laboratory data, imaging, and tissue diagnosis to confirm IMNM while excluding mimics. It also teaches how to interpret inconclusive or distracting findings, such as chronic liver disease, isolated serologies, and borderline cardiac biomarkers.
subtopics: Role of CK, AST, and ALT in evaluating suspected myopathy and separating muscle from liver sources of enzyme elevation
Inflammatory markers and endocrine testing: ESR, CRP, and normal TSH
Broad autoimmune evaluation and the significance of negative ANA, ENA, ANCA, and myositis-specific antibodies
Interpretation of negative anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR testing in suspected IMNM
Clinical meaning and limitations of isolated low-titre SS-B positivity
MRI of the thighs: symmetric proximal muscle oedema as supportive evidence for active myositis
Muscle biopsy findings diagnostic of IMNM: necrotic and regenerating fibres, myophagocytosis, CD68-positive macrophages, sparse CD3-positive T cells, and membrane attack complex staining
Assessment for extramuscular disease: dysphagia, chest imaging for interstitial lung disease, and cardiac testing
Cardiac studies in inflammatory myopathy: troponin, BNP, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI findings suggestive but not definitive for myocarditis
Why repeat liver biopsy and abdominal imaging were useful in confirming persistent steatotic liver disease rather than autoimmune hepatitis or malignancy

sections.section_title: Clinical Reasoning and Differential Diagnosis: Why This Was Seronegative IMNM Probably Triggered by Semaglutide
sections.description: This section focuses on diagnostic synthesis. It compares the leading alternatives, explains why the biopsy and time course favored IMNM over direct toxic rhabdomyolysis or other myopathies, and shows how causality was judged as probable rather than certain.
subtopics: Building the differential diagnosis for proximal weakness with elevated CK and bulbar symptoms
Distinguishing IMNM from acute toxic rhabdomyolysis based on CK trajectory, symptom duration, and need for immunosuppression
Comparison with previously reported GLP-1-related rhabdomyolysis and why this case behaved differently
Excluding statin-associated IMNM through medication history and negative HMGCR antibodies
Why polymyositis and dermatomyositis were less likely: absent rash, biopsy pattern, and serologic profile
Considering endocrine, metabolic, hereditary, infectious, and critical-illness causes of weakness
Interpreting cardiac abnormalities: myocarditis, stress cardiomyopathy, or secondary effects of systemic illness
Assessing whether chronic liver disease could explain the laboratory abnormalities or weakness
Seronegative IMNM as a valid diagnosis despite negative standard myositis antibodies
Applying pharmacovigilance principles and WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre reasoning to label semaglutide as a probable trigger
Key uncertainties and limitations: lack of pre-semaglutide CK, inability to prove causality, and possibility of smouldering pre-existing autoimmunity

sections.description: This section reviews management decisions, monitoring, and outcome, then translates the case into practical teaching points. It emphasizes why this patient received high-intensity initial therapy, how her rapid improvement informed tapering, and what the case means for future prescribing and pharmacovigilance.
subtopics: Initial treatment strategy for severe IMNM: pulse intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisone
Indications for adding IVIG in the setting of persistent weakness and severe bulbar involvement
Supportive care priorities: swallowing safety, mobility, rehabilitation, and monitoring for respiratory compromise
Biochemical and clinical markers of response: CK normalization, improving strength, and return of function
Prednisone tapering guided by sustained remission rather than a fixed schedule
Why additional steroid-sparing immunosuppression or repeat IVIG was not required in this case
Complications during follow-up, including septic shock from pseudomonal urinary infection, and their relevance to immunosuppressed patients
Resolution of possible cardiac involvement and atrial fibrillation on follow-up testing
Long-term outcome: recovery to baseline function and maintenance off immunosuppression with continued avoidance of GLP-1 receptor agonists
How this case informs counseling, drug avoidance, adverse-event reporting, and clinician awareness as semaglutide use expands
